title: Vichyssoise
subtitle: Chilled French leek and potato cream soup
excerpt: The most elegant of cold soups: leeks and potato simmered in chicken stock until completely tender, blended until silky, finished with cream, and served well chilled. Deceptively simple and profoundly satisfying.

recipe.sourceNotes: Vichyssoise is a chilled soup of leeks and potatoes blended with cream, reputedly created by the French-born chef Louis Diat at the Ritz-Carlton in New York around 1917, who claimed to have based it on a leek and potato soup his mother made in Vichy, France. Whether or not the story is accurate, the dish became a classic of refined French-American cooking and remains one of the few cold soups in the classical repertoire. The soup must be blended until completely smooth and passed through a fine sieve for the characteristic silky texture. It is seasoned at the very end after chilling, as cold dulls flavours and the soup will need re-seasoning before serving. Chives are the classic garnish.

content.text: Blend thoroughly and pass through a fine sieve for a perfectly smooth result; a blender alone is not sufficient. The soup must be well chilled before serving (at least 4 hours in the fridge); it should be very cold, not merely cool. Taste and re-season after chilling, as cold temperature suppresses salt and the soup will need more than it did when hot.

items.preparation: white and pale green parts only; sliced

content.text: Melt the butter in a large pot. Add the leeks and onion. Cook over medium-low heat for 10 minutes until very soft and translucent but not coloured. Add the potato and stock. Bring to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes until the potato is completely tender.
Cool slightly. Blend in batches until completely smooth. Pass through a fine sieve, pressing to extract all the liquid. Stir in the cream. Season with salt and white pepper.
Refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight until very cold. Taste and re-season before serving. Ladle into chilled bowls and garnish generously with snipped chives.
